title: Log-rank conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks pose the relation between real matrix rank and deterministic communication, as traced in the checked source papers.
Lovett establishes the general upper bound \(O(\sqrt r\log(r+2))\), substantially improving the linear-rank upper bounds.
Göös, Pitassi and Watson prove a nearly quadratic lower bound in log-rank. Their Theorem 2 first concerns one-sided partition number, with the real-rank consequence stated separately.
Sudakov and Tomon obtain \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r(f)})\). The preprint dates from November 2023, the article appeared online in July 2024, and the journal volume is dated 2025.

Song reports \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) for an explicit construction. This is a preprint claim with a specific quantitative comparison, not an independently verified catalogue assertion of the strongest bound over all constructions.
The checked third revision of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley proves the signed-rectangle decomposition theorem and equivalent formulations, and explicitly retains the general conjecture as open.

status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis

sentences: Alice and Bob must exactly evaluate a total Boolean function while each receives only one part of its input.
The conjecture asks whether their minimum worst-case deterministic communication is bounded by one universal polynomial in logarithmic real matrix rank.
The protocol may use arbitrary interaction and local computation, but all input pairs must be handled correctly.
A refutation must defeat every universal polynomial, rather than a single proposed constant or exponent.
Known square-root-rank upper bounds, nearly quadratic logarithmic lower bounds and signed-partition equivalences leave the central gap unresolved.
